title: Hardik Pandya Leaves Mumbai Behind. The BCCI Centre of Excellence Is Now His Permanent Home.
excerpt: The 32-year-old all-rounder has moved to Bengaluru, hired his own physio and S&C coach, and is paying net bowlers from his own pocket — all to extend his career through the 2027 World Cup and the 2028 LA Olympics.
body:
For the better part of a decade, Hardik Pandya's life orbited Mumbai. The city gave him everything — an IPL franchise in Mumbai Indians, a Lower Parel apartment, and training facilities at the franchise's Ghansoli base. But Mumbai, it seems, has given him all it can.

Pandya has permanently relocated to Bengaluru. He has rented a home on the outskirts of the city, steps from the BCCI's Centre of Excellence — and he intends to make the facility his training headquarters for the rest of his playing career.

"Hardik has already permanently shifted to Bengaluru," a BCCI source told PTI. "He will be the first Indian cricketer to make the COE his permanent training base for the remainder of his career."

## The Logic Behind the Move


![Lower Parel — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/79/Lower_Parel_main_entrance.jpg)


The decision is both practical and strategic. Pandya, 32, is currently recovering from a relapsed quadriceps injury that ruled him out of India's ongoing white-ball tour of the United Kingdom — two T20Is in Ireland and five T20Is against England. He has spent considerable time at the COE over the last six months, and the daily commute from Lower Parel to a training facility in a different part of Mumbai had become unsustainable.

At the COE, he has access to a full suite of resources: injury management, sports science staff, biomechanics labs, and cricket-specific training grounds. But Pandya isn't relying solely on institutional support. He has hired his own physiotherapist and a personal strength and conditioning coach to supplement the COE's programmes. When he does skill work — batting against net bowlers arranged by the facility — he pays them from his own pocket.



> **""Even when he does skill work, such as batting against net bowlers hired by the COE, Hardik pays them from his own pocket," the source added."**


"Even when he does skill work, such as batting against net bowlers hired by the COE, Hardik pays them from his own pocket," the source added.

It is a level of self-funded investment in his own longevity that few Indian cricketers have publicly committed to.


![Centre of Excellence — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/The_Julie_and_Hal_Moore_Center_for_Excellence.jpg/3840px-The_Julie_and_Hal_Moore_Center_for_Excellence.jpg)


## Five to Six More Years

The most striking detail in the reports is Pandya's timeline. He has told people around him that he intends to play white-ball cricket for India for another five to six years — which would take him through the 2027 ODI World Cup in South Africa and Zimbabwe and, crucially, the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, where cricket will return to the Games for the first time in 128 years.

That ambition is what separates this from a routine rehabilitation story. Pandya isn't just trying to get fit for the next series. He is restructuring his entire off-field life around the goal of playing into his late thirties, in a body that has broken down repeatedly.

His injury history is well-documented: back surgery in 2019, ankle issues, shoulder problems, and now recurring quadriceps trouble. The IPL 2026 season saw him miss multiple matches for Mumbai Indians with back spasms and viral fever. The current quad injury is a relapse of the same issue that troubled him during the Afghanistan ODI series earlier this month.


![Mumbai — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/2b/Mumbai_Bandra-Worli_Sea_Link.jpg)


## What Comes Next

Pandya took a brief break from the COE for personal work and is expected to return within days. His rehabilitation is ongoing, and it remains unclear whether he will be available for the three-match T20I series against Zimbabwe, which follows the England tour.

For India, his absence has exposed a familiar vulnerability. With Nitish Kumar Reddy also out — a left quadriceps fibre disruption confirmed on June 23 — the team has no seam-bowling all-rounder available for the entire UK leg. Axar Patel and Washington Sundar are both spinners. The structural gap that Pandya's fitness has masked for years is now fully visible.

## Why This Matters to the Diaspora

The 2028 LA Olympics carry enormous symbolic weight for the Indian diaspora in the United States. Cricket's inclusion in the Games — confirmed by the IOC — means NRIs in Southern California and beyond could watch India play the sport on American soil, in a global sporting event, for the first time. If Pandya's body holds, he could be part of that squad.

His decision to uproot his life, move cities, and invest personally in his fitness infrastructure is not just a career move. It is a bet that the next five years of Indian cricket — World Cups, Olympics, and the continued rise of the white-ball game — are worth building a life around.

For now, the all-rounder trains alone in Bengaluru while his teammates face England without him. The comeback, when it arrives, will be measured not in runs or wickets but in whether the body he is so carefully maintaining can carry him to Los Angeles.
